site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Tukaram's Gentle Sugarcane
body: Walking home along a village road, the poet-saint Tukaram carried a bundle of sugarcane given to him. Children ran up asking for pieces, and he handed them out with a bright smile until only one stalk was left for his family.

At his door, his wife, upset that so little remained, snatched the cane and struck him with it, breaking it into two pieces. Tukaram answered without anger, saying the sugarcane was now fairly split, one piece for each of them.

His gentle reply softened her heart, and the quarrel faded. They sat together, shared the broken stalk as a simple meal, and the home filled again with cheerful harmony and his steady, ungrudging generosity.

stories.title: The Hare Who Became the Moon
stories.source: Sasa Jataka, The Jataka, vol. III, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: In a quiet forest lived a gentle hare alongside a monkey, a jackal, and an otter. When a holy observance day arrived, the hare urged his companions to share food freely with anyone who asked, regardless of station or need.

Sakka, king of the gods, wished to test such a pure heart and descended in the guise of a hungry brahmin. The hare had nothing stored away, yet without hesitation he offered his own body, asking only that a fire be kindled. Sakka created the flames, but when the brave creature leapt into the glowing embers, the fire refused to harm a single hair upon him.

Touched by such willing sacrifice, Sakka revealed himself and praised the hare's boundless generosity. He gently pressed the hare's likeness into the bright face of the full moon, so that all people who gaze upward might remember kindness without measure. The small hare returned unharmed to his beloved forest, carrying warmth back to his waiting friends.

stories.title: The Turtle Who Tricked the Boys
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: By the banks of a sunlit river, a slow turtle was caught by boys who meant to make him their meal. He told them gently that his old shell was far too tough to chew, and begged them to soften him first in the water before cooking.

The boys, believing his calm words, lifted him to the river's edge. The turtle only smiled and asked them to throw him as far out as they could, so the deepest part would do its work, and they swung him high above the sparkling current.

When he splashed down, instead of a frightened meal, the boys watched a joyful swimmer dive beneath the surface. His quick wit had turned their dinner plan into his homecoming, and he slipped away to freedom in the river he loved.

stories.title: The Quiet Wisdom of the Old Gander
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: High in a silk-cotton tree, a colony of ganders made their nests, and one old gander alone watched a slender vine creeping toward the trunk. He warned his flock that the vine would one day become a hunter's stairway, but the younger birds only laughed, too busy with the day to listen to foresight.

Time passed, and the vine grew thick and strong; a hunter climbed it easily and spread his nets among the branches, catching many ganders who thrashed and wept in despair. The old gander, calm as still water, told them to lie limp as though life had left them, and to wait for a single moment of trust.

When the hunter lifted the seemingly lifeless birds and laid them softly on the ground to gather them, the whole flock rose together on quiet wings and flew away. The silk-cotton tree rustled above them, and the colony lived on, saved by patience and the courage to act as one.

stories.title: The Brave Little Bowman
stories.source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
body: A small but skillful bowman joined a wealthy merchant on a journey through a dangerous forest, his slender bow and arrows his only boast. The merchant, used to grand entourages, glanced at the little fellow and wondered aloud how such a quiet companion could ever guard them on the road. Together they pressed onward beneath the towering trees, the bowman watching the shadows with patient, practiced eyes.

Soon a fierce creature burst from the undergrowth, snarling at the travelers, and the merchant cried out in fear. The little bowman did not panic; he drew his bow with steady hands and let fly his arrows one by one, each finding its mark until the beast fled back into the forest. His calm aim saved every soul in the company, and the merchant watched in grateful astonishment.

When the danger had passed, the merchant bowed to his small rescuer and rewarded him generously, ashamed of his earlier doubt. He learned that size and loud boasting are poor measures of worth, while quiet skill and steady courage shine brightest in the hour of need. The brave little bowman walked on, his reputation carried by his arrows and his deeds.
